title: Aeaea in the east: the home of Dawn
greek: νῆσόν τ᾽ Αἰαίην, ὅθι τ᾽ Ἠοῦς ἠριγενείης / οἰκία καὶ χοροί εἰσι καὶ ἀντολαὶ Ἠελίοιο (nēson t' Aiaiēn, hothi t' Ēous ērigeneiēs oikia kai choroi eisi kai antolai Ēelioio)
short: Returning from the dead, Odysseus finds Circe's island at the 'risings of the sun', where Dawn has her house and dancing-floors, though the voyages seemed to lead west.
body: The geography of Books 10-12 is notoriously difficult. The Laestrygonians and the land of the dead lie in the far west, yet Aeaea is placed here at the sunrise. Merry and Riddell review ancient and modern solutions and conclude that Homer imagines the extreme west and the extreme east as almost meeting, a 'point where the darkness and the dawn approach one another' (Gladstone). Nagy speaks of a 'coincidence of opposites' and sees the return from Hades to the place of sunrise as a symbolic rebirth into light; he also suggests that Circe's name may suggest a circle (krikos), and notes that Ēōs, like the Vedic dawn goddess Uṣas, is a dancer. The link with the eastern Argonaut saga (Aeetes in Colchis) may also have pulled Circe's island east.

title: Elpenor's funeral
greek: πήξαμεν ἀκροτάτῳ τύμβῳ εὐῆρες ἐρετμόν (pēxamen akrotatōi tymbōi euēres eretmon)
short: Odysseus fulfils Elpenor's request exactly: cremation with his armour, a mound on the headland, a grave-pillar, and his oar fixed on top.
body: The burial follows the ghost's instructions in 11.72-78 almost word for word, a typical Homeric pattern of command and fulfilment. A heroic funeral in Homer involves the burning of the body, the gathering of the bones, the heaping of a tumulus (tymbos) and the setting up of a stēlē (pillar). The mound 'where the headland runs furthest out to sea' makes it a landmark for sailors, so that the sēma, the 'sign', carries the dead man's memory to 'men yet to be'. Nagy reads the oar as a sign with a double meaning, 'the seafarer is dead' and, in the light of Teiresias' prophecy of the oar taken for a winnowing fan, 'the harvest is complete'. Virgil's Misenus is buried under a mound with his oar and trumpet at Cape Misenum (Aeneid 6.232-235).

title: Disthanees, 'twice-dying'
greek: σχέτλιοι, οἳ ζώοντες ὑπήλθετε δῶμ᾽ Ἀΐδαο, / δισθανέες, ὅτε τ᾽ ἄλλοι ἅπαξ θνῄσκουσ᾽ ἄνθρωποι (schetlioi, hoi zōontes hypēlthete dōm' Aïdao, disthanees, hote t' alloi hapax thnēiskous' anthrōpoi)
short: Circe greets the men as 'twice-dying': having entered Hades alive, they will have to die again, while other men die only once.
body: Disthanēs is a unique word, coined for a unique situation. Circe's address, schetlioi ('rash, hard-hearted ones'), marks the visit to Hades as an act beyond normal human limits, the kind of daring she will rebuke again when Odysseus wants to fight Scylla (12.116-117). Nagy notes that the line looks ahead to Odysseus' real death, foretold by Teiresias, beyond the end of the poem. The idea of a living man's journey to the dead and back, a katabasis, is shared with Heracles, Theseus and Orpheus, and the Nekyia became the model for Aeneas' descent in Aeneid 6 and ultimately for Dante's Commedia.

title: The Sirens
greek: Σειρῆνας μὲν πρῶτον ἀφίξεαι (Seirēnas men prōton aphixeai)
short: Two singers in a flowery meadow, surrounded by the bones of men who listened: whoever hears their song never returns home.
body: Homer says nothing of the Sirens' appearance, only of their voice and of the heap of rotting bones around them; the dual forms (Seirēnoiin, 12.52; 'the two Sirens', 12.167) show that there are two. Their name is of uncertain origin. In Greek art from the seventh century BC they are usually birds with women's heads, as on the famous 'Siren Vase' in the British Museum (c. 480 BC), which shows Odysseus bound to the mast; later writers give them names and parentage (daughters of Achelous). Apollonius of Rhodes has the Argonauts pass them safely because Orpheus drowns their song (Argonautica 4.891-919). Circe's instructions, wax for the crew and ropes for Odysseus, allow him to be the only man to hear the song and survive.

anchor: in the step of the mast
title: Bound to the mast
greek: ὀρθὸν ἐν ἱστοπέδῃ, ἐκ δ᾽ αὐτοῦ πείρατ᾽ ἀνήφθω (orthon en histopedēi, ek d' autou peirat' anēphthō)
short: Odysseus stops his men's ears with softened wax and has himself tied upright to the mast, ordering them to tighten the ropes if he begs to be released.
body: The histopedē is the socket or 'step' in which the mast stands. The scene is told twice, as Circe's instruction and as Odysseus' execution, with the practical detail of warming the wax in the sun and kneading it. It is a perfect image of Odysseus' character: curiosity and self-control at once, achieved by binding himself in advance against a temptation he knows he cannot resist. Philosophers and economists have used it as the model of 'precommitment' (e.g. Jon Elster, Ulysses and the Sirens, 1979). In Dialectic of Enlightenment (1944/1947) Max Horkheimer and Theodor Adorno read the scene as an allegory of modern reason: the master enjoys art in chains while the workers, ears blocked, row on. Odysseus signals with his eyebrows, the only freedom left him (12.193-194).

title: The Sirens' song: knowledge and Iliadic glory
greek: δεῦρ᾽ ἄγ᾽ ἰών, πολύαιν᾽ Ὀδυσεῦ, μέγα κῦδος Ἀχαιῶν ... ἴδμεν γάρ τοι πάνθ᾽ ὅσ᾽ ἐνὶ Τροίῃ εὐρείῃ (deur' ag' iōn, polyain' Odyseu, mega kydos Achaiōn ... idmen gar toi panth' hos' eni Troiēi eureiēi)
short: The Sirens tempt Odysseus not with pleasure but with knowledge: they know all the sufferings at Troy and 'all things that come to pass upon the fruitful earth'.
body: They address him in Iliadic language: 'great glory of the Achaeans' is an Iliadic formula (used of Odysseus at Il. 9.673, 10.544), and polyainos ('much-praised' or, as Nagy argues, 'master of riddling words') is used of him in Il. 9.673 too. Their claim to know everything recalls the Muses, who 'know all things' (Il. 2.485). Nagy calls them 'false Muses': to listen is to be trapped in the past glory of Troy, and Odysseus must sail past the Iliad to secure his nostos. Cicero already saw that the lure was knowledge, translating the lines and observing that the Sirens promised learning so that no one would think they held a wise man by mere songs (De Finibus 5.49). The song itself, only eight lines long, is never heard in its full beauty: Homer gives us its words, not its music.

title: The Planctae, 'Wandering Rocks'
greek: Πλαγκτὰς δή τοι τάς γε θεοὶ μάκαρες καλέουσι (Plangktas dē toi tas ge theoi makares kaleousi)
short: One possible route leads past the Planctae, rocks battered by surf and 'blasts of baneful fire' that no ship has passed except the Argo.
body: Plangktai is normally taken as 'Wanderers' (from plazō, 'wander'), though some ancient and modern scholars preferred 'Clashers' (from plēssō, 'strike'). Merry and Riddell defend 'wandering' and survey the identifications: with the Symplegades, the clashing rocks at the mouth of the Black Sea in the Argonaut story, or with the volcanic Lipari islands near Sicily, whose 'fire' would explain the flames. As with moly, the name is said to be the gods' name. Even the doves that carry ambrosia to Zeus are sometimes caught by the rocks, and Zeus must 'make up the tale' (12.62-65), a mysterious detail. Circe leaves the choice of route to Odysseus, but his narrative passes straight to Scylla and Charybdis, so the Planctae remain unvisited. Apollonius later has the Argo pass them with the help of Thetis (Argonautica 4.922-964).

title: The Argo, 'on the minds of all'
greek: Ἀργὼ πᾶσι μέλουσα, παρ᾽ Αἰήταο πλέουσα (Argō pasi melousa, par' Aiētao pleousa)
short: The only ship to pass the Planctae was the Argo, returning from Aeetes, saved by Hera because she loved Jason: Homer assumes an Argonaut epic already famous.
body: Pasi melousa means literally 'a concern to all', 'on everyone's mind'; Nagy notes that melein is used of the subject of song, so the phrase implies that the Argo's voyage was already a well-known theme of poetry. The lines are important evidence for an early Argonaut epic, older than the Odyssey's final form, on which several of the episodes may draw: Circe is Aeetes' sister, the Laestrygonians' spring Artacia (10.108) has a namesake near Cyzicus on the Argonauts' route, and the Planctae resemble the Clashing Rocks. Karl Meuli (Odyssee und Argonautika, 1921) argued for extensive borrowing from such an Argonautica; the question remains open. Apollonius' Argonautica (3rd century BC) is the version that survives.

title: Scylla
greek: ἔνθα δ᾽ ἐνὶ Σκύλλη ναίει δεινὸν λελακυῖα. / τῆς ἦ τοι φωνὴ μὲν ὅση σκύλακος νεογιλῆς (entha d' eni Skyllē naiei deinon lelakyia. tēs ē toi phōnē men hosē skylakos neogilēs)
short: A cave-dwelling monster with twelve dangling feet, six long necks and six heads with triple rows of teeth, snatching a man with each head.
body: Her voice is like that of a 'new-born whelp' (skylax), a pun on her name. Merry and Riddell think the name originally meant 'the render, tearer' (compare skyllō, 'tear, mangle') and that the link with skylax is a later association, which also explains the dogs that later writers attach to her (Virgil's 'caeruleis canibus', Aeneid 3.432). They compare her to a gigantic octopus or hermit crab fishing from its shell. The ancients located her rock on the Italian side of the Strait of Messina, at Scyllaeum, where the town of Scilla still stands, opposite Charybdis on the Sicilian side. Ovid tells how Circe transformed the nymph Scylla into this monster out of jealousy (Metamorphoses 14.1-74).

title: Charybdis
greek: τῷ δ᾽ ὑπὸ δῖα Χάρυβδις ἀναρροιβδεῖ μέλαν ὕδωρ (tōi d' hypo dia Charybdis anarroibdei melan hydōr)
short: Beneath a fig tree on the lower cliff, Charybdis swallows and spews out the sea three times a day; not even Poseidon could save a ship caught there.
body: Charybdis is a whirlpool personified; the verb anarroibdeō, 'gulp back down', plays on her name. The epithet dia ('divine' or 'bright') is a standard epithet that also marks her as more than natural. Thucydides identifies the strait between Rhegium and Messina as 'the so-called Charybdis' through which Odysseus is said to have sailed (4.24.5), and the currents there are indeed strong, though no whirlpool matches Homer's description. The fig tree is a precise detail that becomes vital later, when Odysseus, swept back on the wreck of his ship, clings to it 'like a bat' until Charybdis spews out his mast and keel (12.432-441). 'Between Scylla and Charybdis' became proverbial for a choice between two dangers.

anchor: deeds of war and on toil
title: Circe's rebuke: no heroics against Scylla
greek: σχέτλιε, καὶ δὴ αὖ τοι πολεμήια ἔργα μέμηλε / καὶ πόνος· οὐδὲ θεοῖσιν ὑπείξεαι ἀθανάτοισιν; (schetlie, kai dē au toi polemēia erga memēle kai ponos; oude theoisin hypeixeai athanatoisin?)
short: Odysseus asks how he can fight Scylla; Circe tells him that she is an immortal evil and that 'to flee from her is bravest'. Better lose six men than all.
body: This exchange states a central difference between the Odyssey and the Iliad. Odysseus' instinct is that of an Iliadic warrior: confront the enemy and protect your men. Circe's answer reverses the heroic code: Scylla is 'not mortal, but an immortal bane', and against her there is no defence; flight is the best courage (phygeein kartiston). The calculation that 'it is better far to mourn six comrades in thy ship than all together' (12.109-110) is a hard arithmetic of survival. When the moment comes, Odysseus 'forgot the hard command of Circe' and armed himself in his 'glorious armour' (12.226-231), a gesture of heroic identity that achieves nothing; he cannot even see the monster. He also keeps silent about Scylla to his crew (12.223-225), a decision that leaders' ethics have debated ever since.

title: Crataiis, mother of Scylla
greek: βωστρεῖν δὲ Κράταιιν, μητέρα τῆς Σκύλλης (bōstrein de Krataiin, mētera tēs Skyllēs)
short: Circe advises Odysseus to call on Crataiis, Scylla's mother, who will keep her from darting out a second time.
body: The name means something like 'the Mighty' (from kratos, 'strength'). Nagy connects it with the word krataiis used of the force that drives back Sisyphus' stone (11.597), suggesting 'having a power that has violence'. Later genealogies give Scylla other parents: Phorcys and Hecate, or Typhon and Echidna (Apollodorus, Epitome 7.20 names Crataiis and Trienus or Phorcus). The advice shows a typical feature of Greek religion: a dangerous power can be controlled by appealing to a higher or related power, here the monster's mother. Odysseus never follows the advice, since he decides to arm himself instead.

title: The cattle of the Sun
greek: ἑπτὰ βοῶν ἀγέλαι, τόσα δ᾽ οἰῶν πώεα καλά, / πεντήκοντα δ᾽ ἕκαστα. γόνος δ᾽ οὐ γίγνεται αὐτῶν, / οὐδέ ποτε φθινύθουσι (hepta boōn agelai, tosa d' oiōn pōea kala, pentēkonta d' hekasta. gonos d' ou gignetai autōn, oude pote phthinythousi)
short: On Thrinacia graze seven herds of cattle and seven flocks of sheep, fifty in each; they never breed and never die. To touch them is fatal.
body: Seven herds of fifty make 350, close to the number of days in the lunar year. Merry and Riddell report, from Eustathius, that Aristotle interpreted the cattle as the days of the year, unchanging in number, but they decline to follow the allegory; they note that Greek sanctuaries really did keep herds sacred to gods, citing Herodotus' account of the Sun's flocks at Apollonia (9.93), and mention the Vedic image of the sun's rays as cows. The cattle are the subject of the poem's first lines: the companions perished because they 'devoured the cattle of Helios Hyperion' (1.8-9). The episode is thus the climax that the proem announced, and the test that Teiresias and Circe both set (11.104-115, 12.137-141).

title: Phaethusa and Lampetie, the Sun's daughters
greek: νύμφαι ἐϋπλόκαμοι, Φαέθουσά τε Λαμπετίη τε, / ἃς τέκεν Ἠελίῳ Ὑπερίονι δῖα Νέαιρα (nymphai eüplokamoi, Phaethousa te Lampetiē te, has teken Ēeliōi Hyperioni dia Neaira)
short: The cattle are herded by two nymphs whose names mean 'Shining' and 'Radiant', daughters of Helios by Neaera ('the Young One').
body: Phaethousa comes from phaethō, 'shine' (compare Phaethon), and Lampetiē from lampō, 'beam'. Nagy compares the names of the horses of Dawn, Lampos and Phaethon (23.246), and places them in a wider Indo-European mythology of light. Neaera means 'new' or 'young', fitting a mother of light-maidens. Lampetie plays an active role later: she runs to tell her father that the cattle have been killed (12.374-375). In later myth the Heliades, daughters of the Sun, are the sisters of Phaethon who were turned into poplars weeping amber after his fall (Ovid, Metamorphoses 2.340-366); Ovid names Phaethusa and Lampetie among them.

title: Helios Hyperion
greek: αὐγὴ Ἠελίου Ὑπεριονίδαο ἄνακτος (augē Ēeliou Hyperionidao anaktos)
short: Hyperion, 'he who goes above', is used both as a title of the Sun himself and, as here in the Greek, for the Sun's father.
body: In the line describing the sun's heat softening the wax, the Greek calls Helios Hyperionidēs, 'son of Hyperion', while elsewhere (1.8, 12.133, 12.346) he is Hēlios Hyperiōn, as if Hyperion were his own name or epithet. Murray translates both as 'Helios Hyperion'. Hesiod makes Hyperion one of the Titans, father of Helios, Selene (Moon) and Eos (Dawn) (Theogony 371-374). Nagy explains the name as 'the one who travels up above', fitting both father and son. The repeated naming of the Sun with this full title in Book 12 marks the rising importance of the god whose cattle will destroy the crew.

title: 'One day we shall remember these things too'
greek: καί που τῶνδε μνήσεσθαι ὀίω (kai pou tōnde mnēsesthai oiō)
short: Odysseus encourages his frightened men by recalling their escape from the Cyclops and predicting that they will one day remember this danger too.
body: The speech is a model of leadership under pressure: it recalls a past success, claims credit for it ('through my valor and counsel and wit'), predicts survival, and gives clear orders to rowers and helmsman. But it is also a deception, since Odysseus deliberately says nothing of Scylla. Virgil adapted the consolation in Aeneas' speech to his storm-tossed men, 'forsan et haec olim meminisse iuvabit', 'perhaps one day it will be a pleasure to remember even these things' (Aeneid 1.198-207, line 203), adding the note of pleasure in remembered suffering. The Odyssey itself develops that idea elsewhere: Eumaeus says that a man who has suffered much takes delight in his sorrows afterwards (15.400-401).

anchor: a fisher on a jutting rock
title: The angler and the six men taken by Scylla
greek: ὡς δ᾽ ὅτ᾽ ἐπὶ προβόλῳ ἁλιεὺς περιμήκεϊ ῥάβδῳ ... ἐς πόντον προΐησι βοὸς κέρας ἀγραύλοιο (hōs d' hot' epi probolōi halieus perimēkei rhabdōi ... es ponton proiēsi boos keras agrauloio)
short: Scylla snatches six men, who cry Odysseus' name for the last time as they are drawn up writhing, like fish landed by a fisherman with rod and line.
body: The 'horn of an ox' is a piece of horn tubing on the line just above the hook, to stop fish biting through it; the same detail occurs in the Iliad (Il. 24.80-82). The simile reverses the usual relation of man and nature, as in the Laestrygonians' spearing of men 'like fishes' (10.124). The men are 'the best in strength and in might', and they call on Odysseus 'by name for that last time': the narrator's memory is personal. Odysseus' judgement, 'Most piteous did mine eyes behold that thing of all that I bore' (12.258-259), is one of the few places where he ranks his sufferings. Scylla's taking of six men fulfils Circe's warning exactly (12.109-110).

title: 'You are made of iron': Eurylochus' protest
greek: σχέτλιός εἰς, Ὀδυσεῦ, περί τοι μένος, οὐδέ τι γυῖα / κάμνεις· ἦ ῥά νυ σοί γε σιδήρεα πάντα τέτυκται (schetlios eis, Odyseu, peri toi menos, oude ti guia kamneis; ē rha ny soi ge sidērea panta tetyktai)
short: When Odysseus orders them to sail past Thrinacia, Eurylochus answers bitterly that their leader is made of iron and does not feel his men's exhaustion.
body: Schetlios, Murray's 'Hardy', also means 'stubborn, cruel'. The image of a man made of iron expresses both admiration and reproach: Odysseus' endurance is superhuman, but he ignores the needs of ordinary men. In the Iliad iron is used of an unbending heart (Hecuba to Priam, Il. 24.205, 'surely your heart is of iron'). Eurylochus' argument is not foolish: night winds are dangerous and the men are exhausted. The other comrades agree, and Odysseus, outvoted, sees that 'some god was assuredly devising ill' (12.295). His only recourse is to bind them by an oath not to touch the cattle (12.298-304). Readers often find Eurylochus' speech the most human voice among the crew.

anchor: All forms of death are hateful
title: Eurylochus' speech: death by hunger is the worst
greek: πάντες μὲν στυγεροὶ θάνατοι δειλοῖσι βροτοῖσι, / λιμῷ δ᾽ οἴκτιστον θανέειν καὶ πότμον ἐπισπεῖν (pantes men stygeroi thanatoi deiloisi brotoisi, limōi d' oiktiston thaneein kai potmon epispein)
short: Starving after a month of contrary winds, the crew are persuaded by Eurylochus to sacrifice the best of the cattle and promise Helios a temple in Ithaca.
body: The speech is a small masterpiece of persuasion. It begins with a general truth (all deaths are hateful, hunger the most pitiable), proposes a pious-seeming solution (sacrifice to the gods, a temple to Helios on their return), and ends with a defiant choice of a quick death at sea over slow wasting 'in a desert isle'. It is spoken while Odysseus sleeps (12.338), as when the bag of winds was opened. Ironically it contains the truth about the alternatives: the crew will indeed lose their lives 'once for all' in the sea. The proem judged the act as the comrades' own folly (atasthaliai, 1.7), and Zeus's opening speech (1.32-34) insists that humans suffer 'beyond their lot' through their own recklessness.

title: A sacrifice gone wrong
greek: φύλλα ... δρυὸς ὑψικόμοιο· / οὐ γὰρ ἔχον κρῖ λευκὸν ἐϋσσέλμου ἐπὶ νηός ... ἀλλ᾽ ὕδατι σπένδοντες (phylla ... dryos hypsikomoio; ou gar echon kri leukon eüsselmou epi nēos ... all' hydati spendontes)
short: The crew go through the forms of sacrifice, but with oak leaves instead of barley and water instead of wine, on animals that belong to a god.
body: A normal Homeric sacrifice (e.g. Il. 1.447-474, Od. 3.430-463) begins with the scattering of barley grains (oulochytai) and prayer, then the cutting of throats, the burning of the thigh-pieces wrapped in fat as the gods' portion, libations of wine, and the tasting of the entrails (splanchna) before the feast. Every step is here, but the substitutions mark the ritual as defective, and the victims are sacred property of Helios. The crew's 'sacrifice' is really a theft dressed as worship. The wording echoes Odysseus' own sacrifice of the Cyclops' ram, which Zeus also rejected (9.551-555). Odysseus, waking, smells the roasting fat and knows at once that his 'pitiless sleep' was a divine trap (12.369-373).

title: Helios' threat to shine among the dead
greek: δύσομαι εἰς Ἀΐδαο καὶ ἐν νεκύεσσι φαείνω (dysomai eis Aïdao kai en nekyessi phaeinō)
short: Told by Lampetie of the slaughter, Helios demands vengeance and threatens to abandon the living world for the dead; Zeus promises to destroy the ship.
body: The threat shows what is at stake: if the gods' honour (timē) is not respected, the order of the cosmos itself could collapse. The Sun's daily path between heaven and earth is what makes life possible, and to shine in Hades would reverse light and darkness. Zeus restores order by agreeing to strike the ship with his thunderbolt. The scene raises the poem's question of divine justice: the crew have broken an oath and robbed a god, and their punishment is presented as deserved, in contrast to Odysseus' innocent sufferings at Poseidon's hands. Note the 'all-seeing' Sun (11.109) must be told by his daughter what has happened, a detail that critics have found either naive or wryly ironic.

anchor: This I heard from fair-haired Calypso
title: How Odysseus knows what the gods said
greek: ταῦτα δ᾽ ἐγὼν ἤκουσα Καλυψοῦς ἠϋκόμοιο· / ἡ δ᾽ ἔφη Ἑρμείαο διακτόρου αὐτὴ ἀκοῦσαι (tauta d' egōn ēkousa Kalypsous ēykomoio; hē d' ephē Hermeiao diaktorou autē akousai)
short: Odysseus explains that he learned of the divine conversation from Calypso, who heard it from Hermes, so his first-person narrative stays consistent.
body: In the Apologoi Odysseus can report only what he saw, heard or was told. A council between Helios and Zeus lies outside his experience, so he gives his source, a chain of informants reaching from Hermes to Calypso to himself. The lines show the poet's (or the narrator's) awareness of the limits of first-person narrative. Readers have nonetheless found the explanation awkward: Hermes is not shown telling Calypso this in Book 5, and the scene on Olympus is narrated with a fullness that seems more like the poet's omniscience than hearsay. The passage is often discussed in modern narratology as a sign of the care with which the Apologoi are framed as Odysseus' own account.

title: The portents: crawling hides and lowing meat
greek: εἷρπον μὲν ῥινοί, κρέα δ᾽ ἀμφ᾽ ὀβελοῖσι μεμύκει, / ὀπταλέα τε καὶ ὠμά, βοῶν δ᾽ ὣς γίγνετο φωνή (heirpon men rhinoi, krea d' amph' obeloisi memykei, optalea te kai ōma, boōn d' hōs gigneto phōnē)
short: The gods send uncanny signs: the flayed hides creep, and the meat on the spits, roast and raw, moos like living cattle. The men feast on for six days.
body: This is one of the strangest moments in Homer, a supernatural horror quite unlike the realism of the Iliad. The animals seem to live on in their dismembered parts, as if the god's property could not really be consumed. The portents are 'shown forth' (teraa prouphainon) for the men, a warning they ignore: they go on eating for six days until the wind changes. Readers have compared the episode with the prodigies before the suitors' death, when the suitors laugh with 'alien jaws' and eat meat 'spattered with blood' (20.345-357). In both cases a feast on stolen goods becomes a sign of approaching destruction.

title: The shipwreck: 'the god took away their return'
greek: θεὸς δ᾽ ἀποαίνυτο νόστον (theos d' apoainyto noston)
short: Zeus' thunderbolt shatters the ship; the helmsman falls 'like a diver', the men float 'like sea-crows', and the god takes away their homecoming.
body: The half-line repeats the proem almost exactly: of the companions it said that Helios 'took from them the day of their returning' (1.9). Book 12 thus closes the circle opened in the first lines of the poem: the companions' nostos is lost, and Odysseus alone survives. The two similes are brief and grim: the pilot, struck by the falling mast, drops from the deck like a diver (arneutēr), and the men bob among the waves like sea-birds (korōnai einaliai). The same lines reappear almost word for word in one of Odysseus' false tales in Ithaca (14.301-309), and the solitary survival on mast and keel prepares the parallel shipwreck of Book 5, which in the poem's order the audience has already heard.

anchor: clung to it like a bat
title: Clinging to the fig tree like a bat
greek: τῷ προσφὺς ἐχόμην ὡς νυκτερίς (tōi prosphys echomēn hōs nykteris)
short: Carried back to Charybdis on his makeshift raft, Odysseus leaps up to the fig tree and hangs from it like a bat, waiting for the whirlpool to return his timbers.
body: The South Wind drives him back through the strait, so that he must face Charybdis after all, the danger he had avoided by choosing Scylla's side. The bat simile is unusual and exact: a bat hangs from a branch with nothing beneath its feet, as Odysseus does, unable to climb up or rest on the roots, which are far below. The fig tree mentioned by Circe (12.103) now becomes the instrument of survival. Bats appear elsewhere in Homer as an image for the gibbering souls of the dead suitors flitting into Hades (24.6-9), so the comparison may also suggest how close Odysseus is to death.

title: Time measured by a judge's supper
greek: ἦμος δ᾽ ἐπὶ δόρπον ἀνὴρ ἀγορῆθεν ἀνέστη / κρίνων νείκεα πολλὰ δικαζομένων αἰζηῶν (ēmos d' epi dorpon anēr agorēthen anestē krinōn neikea polla dikazomenōn aizēōn)
short: The mast and keel reappear at the hour when a judge, having decided many young men's quarrels, gets up from the assembly to go to supper.
body: Like 'the time for unyoking oxen' (9.58) and the woodcutter's meal-time in the Iliad (Il. 11.86-89), this is a time-reference drawn from everyday civic life. Its placement is striking: at the moment of greatest peril, clinging to a tree above a whirlpool, Odysseus measures the long wait by the peaceful routine of a city's law-court. The contrast underlines his isolation from the ordered human community and his longing for it. The image of the judge settling disputes (dikazō, krinō) recalls the trial scene on Akhilleus' shield (Il. 18.497-508).

title: The end of the Apologoi: 'a tale plainly told'
greek: ἐχθρὸν δέ μοί ἐστιν / αὖτις ἀριζήλως εἰρημένα μυθολογεύειν (echthron de moi estin autis arizēlōs eirēmena mythologeuein)
short: Nine more days bring Odysseus to Ogygia; he stops there, since he told the Calypso story yesterday, and 'it is irksome to tell again a tale plainly told'.
body: The ending closes the narrative in a ring. The story has reached the point where Odysseus' account to Arete began in Book 7 (7.244-266), and the epic itself began with Odysseus on Calypso's island (Books 1 and 5). Nagy notes that the return from Calypso's cave completes a series of escapes from enclosed places, the Cyclops' cave and Hades. The refusal to repeat a story is also a neat narrator's touch from a man who will, in Ithaca, tell several false versions of his life. Arizēlōs means 'very clearly, distinctly'. Book 13 begins with the Phaeacians' enchanted silence, repeating the lines of the Intermezzo (13.1-2 = 11.333-334), and the gifts and voyage home follow.
